Cardiovascular Physiology
The cardiovascular system has three fundamental parts:
-the heart: a pump providing the blood with the energy necessary for its flow to the tissuees;
-blood vessels: the communication pathways by which blood circulates from the heart to the tissuees and returns there;
-blood: liquid medium in which materials (O₂, CO₂, nutrients, waste, etc.) and cells are transported.

I-Coordination of cardiac function
The heart is a dual pump, in that its right and left sides pump blood separately, but simultaneously, into the systemic and pulmonary circulations.
Effective blood pumping requires contraction first of the atria, followed almost immediately by contraction of the ventricles.
I-Coordination of cardiac function
Cardiac muscle contraction is triggered by depolarization of the plasma membrane.
Junctions connect myocardial cells and ensure the propagation of action potentials from one cell to another.
An initial excitation of one heart cell results in the excitation of all cells of the heart.
This initial depolarization normally originates in the sinus node (SNA) and propagates throughout all of the atria and then throughout all of the ventricles.
I-Coordination of cardiac function
The evolution of all phenomena of cardiac activity occurring between two successive cardiac contractions corresponds to the cardiac cycle.
Following an immutable order of occurrence, electrical phenomena always precede mechanical phenomena.
The cardiac cycle includes a phase of activity (depolarization and contraction) called systole and a rest phase (repolarization and relaxation) called diastole.
Cardiac electrophysiologyI-Coordination of cardiac function
II-Electrical properties of the heart
Three types of cells can be individualized in the myocardium.
Contractile cells largely predominate and ensure contraction.
The other cells, of two types, are less numerous without clear contractile characteristics:
-the conductive or cardionector cells are capable of spontaneously depolarizing and rapidly transmitting this depolarization, they constitute the conduction tissuee;
-myoendocrine cells, located mainly in auricular tissuee, secrete natriuretic factors and are involved in the regulation of sodium balance.
Excito-conductive or cardionector tissuee
Internodal beams
II- Electrical properties of the heart:
A-Excitability:
All myocardial cells are excitable, that is to say, when they are sufficiently stimulated, they respond with depolarization followed, depending on the case, by contraction.
But, even from a purely electrical aspect, there is a significant difference in behavior between cardiomyocytes located in different regions of the heart.

1-Polarization: membrane potential

1-Polarization: membrane potential
At rest, myocardial cells are polarized, with a predominance of positive charges on the outside and negative charges on the inside.

If two microelectrodes connected to a galvanometer are placed, one extracellular and the other intracellular, a potential difference is recorded, different depending on the cell type at around – 80 mV for a ventricular cell, it is the transmembrane resting potential which is determined by the potassium conductance.
II- Electrical properties of the heart:
A-Excitability
2-Elementary electrical activity: the action potential (PA)
The potential variations at the origin of the PA depend on the incoming (depolarizing) and outgoing (repolarizing) ionic currents occurring in a determined order.
II- Electrical properties of the heart:
2-Elementary electrical activity: the action potential
There are two main types of cardiac BP:
-PA of rapidly depolarizing cells: ventricular myocardium, atrial myocardium, His bundle and Purkinje network;
-PA of slowly depolarizing cells or slow PA: sinus and atrioventricular nodes.

Phase 0: rapid depolarization.
When a depolarization wave arrives in a contractile cell through the gap junctions the membrane potential becomes positive (+).
Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open, resulting in rapid entry of Na⁺ into the cell. The membrane potential reverses and reaches approximately +20mV to +30mV before inactivation of the Na⁺ channels.
The activation of the sodium current (INa) is extremely rapid, of the order of 1 ms, while the inactivation is slower, of the order of 10 to 15 ms.

blocks.text: The PA of rapidly depolarizing cells has four phases Example: PA of a ventricular contractile cell
Phase 1: Start of repolarization (rapid initial repolarization).
Inactivation of Na⁺ channels: a small fraction of sodium channels only slowly inactivate, participating in the PA plateau.
The cell begins to repolarize thanks to a transient potassium current flowing out through the opening of fast voltage-gated K⁺ channels.

blocks.text: The PA of rapidly depolarizing cells has four phases Example: PA of a ventricular contractile cell
Phase 2: plateau.

The prolonged plateau results from a slower but more lasting opening of voltage-dependent Ca²⁺ channels: L-type Ca²⁺ channels (L for long lasting or long term) also called dihydropyridine receptors, DHPR in English because they are specifically closed by these substances.
These channels are activated by depolarization and open slowly during phases 0 and 1. When their opening is completed, Ca²⁺enters the cell.

Phase 2: plateau.
Regulation of calcium current: acceleration of heart rate and β-adrenergic stimulation increase the entry of calcium into the cell.
Three main classes of organic blockers or calcium antagonists have been identified:
-dihydropyridines (nifedipine);
-benzothiazepines (diltiazem);
-phenylalkylamines (verapamil).

Closure of L-type Ca²⁺ channels and opening of other K⁺ channel subtypes. There is then a rapid release of K⁺ and the cell returns to resting potential.

Roles of the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger and the Na⁺, K⁺ ATPase pump in the PA of a ventricular cell:
1- Role of the Na⁺/Ca²⁺(NCX) exchanger:

NCX transports Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ ions across the cell membrane along concentration gradients. This system exchanges three sodium ions for one calcium ion, i.e., in summary, the movement of a positive charge.
Depending on the direction of the exchange, the resulting current is inward and depolarizing or outward and repolarizing.

Roles of the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger and the Na⁺, K⁺ ATPase pump in the PA of a ventricular cell:
1- Role of the Na⁺/Ca²⁺(NCX) exchanger:
The direction of the current is determined by the membrane potential, the exchange current is:
- outgoing (exit of Na⁺ and entry of Ca²⁺) at the very beginning of the PA;
- then mainly incoming (entrance of Na⁺ and exit of Ca²⁺) participating in the PA plateau;
- finally entering participating in the control of intracellular calcium concentration, particularly during diastole.

2- Role of the Na⁺, K⁺ ATPase pump

The Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase sodium pump ensures active transport of ions across the cell membrane. Two potassium ions enter the cell for every three sodium ions leaving, giving a total of one repolarizing outgoing current.
The sodium pump intervenes at the end of the PA and tends to hyperpolarize the membrane. It is activated in the event of intracellular sodium overload

Ventricular electrophysiological heterogeneity:
The recording of ventricular action potentials in several ventricular sites revealed very different APs.
These differences are mainly explained by the heterogeneity of myocardial distribution of potassium channels.
This heterogeneity exists between the right and left ventricles, the apex and base of the ventricles and within the wall itself.

Concept of refractory period
The contractile response of the heart muscle begins just after the onset of depolarization.

During phases 0 to 2 and for almost half of phase 3 (until the membrane potential reaches approximately -50mV during repolarization), the heart muscle cannot be excited again regardless of the intensity of the current. It is then in its absolute refractory period (PRA)

pages.title: The Action Potential of Slowly Depolarizing Cells

blocks.text: The Action Potential of Slowly Depolarizing Cells
Phase 4: pacemaker potential (rather than resting potential); slow spontaneous depolarization or pre-potential.
At approximately -65mv potential, the current K⁺ (IK) decreases and leads to the activation of channels allowing the passage of Na⁺ and K⁺.
These channels are called “f” channels because of their unusual “funny” activity.
When these channels open, the membrane potential being negative, the entry of Na⁺ prevails over the exit of K⁺.

The membrane begins to depolarize forming the first part of the pre-potential, which leads to the closure of the “f” channels, the opening of the calcium channels T (for transients) and the L channels (for long-term opening).
The ICa T completes the pre-potential to the threshold.

blocks.text: The Action Potential of Slowly Depolarizing Cells
Phase 0: depolarization.
Once the threshold is reached (-45mV), the incoming calcium current (ICa) due to the opening of L-type calcium channels (for long-term opening) triggers the influx (PA).
Phase 3: repolarization
When the Ca²⁺ channels close at the peak of the PA, the outgoing IK begins and leads to repolarization thanks to the opening of the K⁺ channels.

blocks.text: The Action Potential of Slowly Depolarizing Cells
Slow diastolic depolarization of sinus cells (see diagram: sinus node action potential)
Slow diastolic membrane depolarization is characteristic of cells responsible for cardiac automaticity; it governs the heart rate under the control of two interdependent clocks:
-a sequential cascade of opening of voltage-gated or non-voltage-dependent membrane ion channels (membrane clock model);
- intracellular calcium movements via the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger (calcium clock model).

pages.title: The Action Potential of Slowly Depolarizing Cells

blocks.text: The Action Potential of Slowly Depolarizing Cells
Role of the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger in the sinus node (see diagram: action potential of the sinus node and its different ionic currents)
During diastole, calcium channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum spontaneously and rhythmically release calcium into the cytosol.
This increase in intracellular calcium activates the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger, creating a depolarizing sodium current which contributes to the end of slow diastolic depolarization.
This sodium depolarizing current represents the calcium clock of automation.
II- Electrical properties of the heart:
B-Diastolic (resting) potential and cardiac automatism
Placed outside the body, that is to say entirely disconnected from the nervous system and hormones, the heart continues to beat.
This mechanical automatism is, fundamentally, an electrical phenomenon: a spontaneous cellular depolarization.
All cells of the conduction system are automatic, if their transmembrane potential is recorded, slow spontaneous diastolic depolarization (DDL) is observed.
DDL is linked to spontaneous ion exchanges.
DDL allows the membrane potential to spontaneously reach the depolarization threshold.
II- Electrical properties of the heart:
B-Diastolic (resting) potential and cardiac automatism
The steeper the slope of the DDL, the more easily the depolarization threshold is reached, and the more the discharge frequency of the cardiac cell is accelerated.
The cells of the sinus node present the fastest automatism (steeper DOF slope) and therefore control the heart rate. The sinus node is the physiological pacemaker or true pacemaker.
The other automatic cells are latent pacemakers with a slower discharge frequency.

II- Electrical properties of the heart:
C-Conduction:

Conduction at the cardiac tissuee level requires the transmission of PA from one cell to the neighboring cell. The possibility of this transmission and its speed depend on the structural and functional properties:
-anatomical obstacles;
-the geometry and diameter of the cells;
-intercellular connections (gap type junctions);
-the distribution and expressure of ion channels along the cell membrane and in the intercalated discs;
All these elements contribute to the heterogeneity of conduction in the myocardium.
II- Electrical properties of the heart:
C-Conduction
Under physiological conditions, the conductance of gap junctions is one of the most relevant parameters in the regulation of conduction within cardiac tissuee.

Their heterogeneous distribution on the surface of the membrane ensures a complex three-dimensional intercellular electrical coupling with a propagation speed depending on the number of gap junctions and the type of connexin or connexins that compose them.
II- Electrical properties of the heart:
C-Conduction:
1-In the earpieces:
The depolarization appearing in the NSA propagates radially in the muscle fibers which constitute the atria. The conduction velocity (Vc) of the auricular tissuee is approximately 0.3m/s.
The internodal conduction bundles ensure the conduction of impulses to the atrioventricular node (AVN), there are 3 of them: anterior, middle and posterior. Their Vc is 1m/s.
Excito-conductive or cardionector tissuee
Internodal beams
II- Electrical properties of the heart:
C-Conduction:
2-In the NAV:
There is a slowdown in conduction, the time to cross the NAV is 0.09s.
This slowing of conduction is the cause of the gap between the contraction of the atria and the contraction of the ventricles.
II- Electrical properties of the heart:
C- Conduction:
2-In the AV node
For atrial contraction to be effective in terms of filling the ventricles, it must occur while the ventricles are relaxed and the atrioventricular valves are open.
This slowdown is linked to:
- the small diameter of the cells which constitute the AVN (the smallest diameter in conduction tissuee);
-the rarity of communicating junctions between neighboring cells at this level.
- the presence of variable quantities of connexin type 45 and connexin type 30.2.

blocks.text: II- Electrical properties of the heart:
C-Conduction:
3-In the cells of the His-purkinje conduction tissuee
The Vc is highest in conduction tissuee from 3 to 5m/s (5m/s in Purkinje fibers): 150 times > Vc of the NAV.
Transmission is instantaneous throughout both ventricles. This speed of transmission is linked to:
-the large size of the fibers of this fabric;
-the high permeability of the junctions between adjacent conducting cells;
-the significant presence of connexin type 40.
II- Electrical properties of the heart:
C-Conduction:
3-In the cells of the His-purkinje conduction tissuee
Each branch of the His bundle gradually divides into a network of fine ramifications: the Purkinje fibers, which travel under the subendocardial region and reach the myocardial muscle cells.
The duration of passage of the impulse between the common trunk of the bundle of His and the Purkinje fibers is approximately 0.03 s.
II- Electrical properties of the heart:
C-Conduction:
4-In ventricular muscle cells
Once it reaches the end of the Purkinje network, the impulse is transmitted to all the ventricular muscle cells: from ventricular muscle cell to ventricular muscle cell with a Vc of 0.5m/s.

The impulse passes from the endocardium to the epicardium with a delay of 0.03s, so the contraction of the endocardial region precedes the contraction of the epicardial region by a few hundredths of a second.

blocks.text: II- Electrical properties of the heart:
D- Excitation-contraction coupling (electromechanical coupling):
The self-excitation of a single cell (pacemaker) leads to the synchronous contraction of all the cells of the myocardium which behaves like a syncytium (functional = electrical = pseudosyncytium)
In ventricular cells, the ICaL current (extracellular Ca²⁺ entering the cell through L-type calcium channels):
maintains membrane depolarization during the AP plateau;
and triggers the release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (a phenomenon called calcium-induced calcium release).
II- Electrical properties of the heart:
D- Excitation-contraction coupling (electromechanical coupling):
Calcium released into the cytoplasm by the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) binds to contractile proteins and triggers contraction.
L-type calcium channels are thus at the center of excitation–contraction coupling.
II- Electrical properties of the heart:
D- Excitation-contraction coupling (electromechanical coupling):
The binding of external Ca²⁺ to ryanodine receptors opens the calcium channels of the RS (these channels are closed by ryanodine) and the Ca²⁺ of the RS is released.
Ryanodine receptors are Ca²⁺ channels whose opening is responsible for Ca²⁺-induced release of Ca²⁺.
II- Electrical properties of the heart:
D- Excitation-contraction coupling (electromechanical coupling):
Once released, the intracellular Ca²⁺ is stored again in the RS by the Ca²⁺ATPase pump of the RS.
It is this pumping of Ca²⁺ into the RS which allows the relaxation of the sacromeres: this is the initiating event of cardiac diastole.

III- Influence of the autonomic nervous system on cardiac electrophysiology: control of the spontaneous activity of the sinus node

In the absence of any nervous or hormonal influence on the NSA, the rhythmic beating of the heart occurs at a frequency of approximately 100 beats/min: this is the spontaneous inherent discharge frequency of the NSA.
Parasympathetic stimulation decreases heart rate (HR) and sympathetic stimulation increases it.
At rest, parasympathetic activity predominates and resting HR = 70 beats/min
The sympathetic (accelerator) and parasympathetic (braking) systems will constantly modulate the frequency of contraction (chronotropism).
III- Influence of the autonomic nervous system on cardiac electrophysiology: control of the spontaneous activity of the sinus node

The sinus node region is richly innervated with a high density of adrenergic receptors (β₁ and β₂) and muscarinic M₂ receptors. The pacemaker current INaf is the main target of neurotransmitters; the current ICa,T is insensitive to them.

Intracellular cAMP is central to the regulation of INaf by neurotransmitters. cAMP acts directly on the INaf channel equipped with a specific receptor, located on the cytoplasmic carboxyterminal part.
III- Influence of the autonomic nervous system on cardiac electrophysiology: control of the spontaneous activity of the sinus node
The increase in cAMP results in an increase in the INaf current, an increase in the slope of the DDL and, therefore, an acceleration in the heart rate and vice versa for a decrease in cAMP.
Sympathetic nerve endings release norepinephrine: norepinephrine increases the intracellular concentration of cAMP.
Conversely, parasympathetic nerve endings release acetylcholine: acetylcholine reduces the intracellular concentration of cAMP.
III- Influence of the autonomic nervous system on cardiac electrophysiology: control of the spontaneous activity of the sinus node
For the ICaL current which contributes to the terminal part of the diastolic potential; its activation by catecholamines accelerates the rhythm (accelerates the depolarization phase = phase 0).

blocks.text: IV- Heart rhythm abnormalities

In normal subjects, each contraction is triggered in the sinus node (normal sinus rhythm). The frequency decreases (bradycardia) during sleep and increases (tachycardia) under the influence of emotions, exercise, fever and many other stimuli.
Dysfunction of the NSA, induced by drugs or diseases, can reduce or even eliminate the transmission of PA from the atria to the ventricles.

In this case, the cells capable of autorhythmicity of the AVN, the His bundle and the Purkinje network, which are no longer driven by the NSA, begin to generate excitations at their own inherent rhythm, thus becoming the pacemaker of the ventricles. This rhythm is quite slow, from 25 to 40 beats/min.
IV- Heart rhythm abnormalities
Also, when the AVN is blocked, all synchronism with the atrial contractions disappears, these maintaining the normal, higher rhythm of the NSA.

The current treatment for all severe atrioventricular conduction disorders, as well as many other abnormal rhythms, is the permanent surgical implantation of an artificial pacemaker that electrically stimulates the ventricular cells at a normal rhythm.
Conclusion

In the heart, contractions are controlled by a well-regulated cascade of electrical signal transmission that begins in the NSA and passes through the atrial muscle tissuee and then throughout the conduction tissuee to reach the ventricles. The propagation of the electrical signal from one cell to another takes place through gap junctions. The speed of propagation depends on anatomical characteristics, but it can also be modified by a nerve impulse.
